influences.name: 100 gecs
influences.context: rekindling his interest through listening to hyperpop duo 100 gecs

influences.name: Underscores
influences.context: His perspective shifted after discovering newer artists, including Underscores and her studio album Wallsocket (2023)

influences.name: Sophie
influences.context: he recalled discovering Sophie's 2014 song 'Bipp', believing it was 'where grime was gonna go next'

influences.name: Dorian Electra
influences.context: While he first explored hyperpop with a Dorian Electra collaboration in 2021

influences.name: Angel Prost
influences.context: He was inspired further by Angel Prost of hyperpop duo Frost Children, who recorded spoken word interludes throughout the album

influences.name: Quadeca
influences.context: Encouraged by folktronica musician Quadeca, Brown also relearned how to write songs through Julia Cameron's self-help book The Artist's Way

influences.name: Prince
influences.context: Brown named the alter ego 'Dusty Star', likening it to Prince's album Purple Rain (1984)

influences.name: Charli XCX
influences.context: The album draws on a wide palette of influences, including 'grime-meets-Charli XCX glitchiness'

influences.name: Dizzee Rascal
influences.context: The ninth track, 'Baby', featuring Underscores, takes inspiration from Dizzee Rascal's grime production, specifically the 'double claps, helium-high squeaks', and 'car-speaker basslines' of his 2003 track 'I Luv U'

influences.name: Drain Gang
influences.context: reminiscent of the production of the Swedish cloud rap collective Drain Gang

influences.name: Atari Teenage Riot
influences.context: the song draws similarities to German digital hardcore band Atari Teenage Riot

influences.name: Radiohead
influences.context: I made XXX with the aim of getting great reviews. And when I started making Old, I was trying to think of artists that came back from getting great reviews and made an album that was just as good—or better! The only group I could really come up with was Radiohead.

influences.name: Radiohead (Kid A)
influences.context: So if XXX was my OK Computer, then I'd have to make my Kid A next. So I studied Kid A, and I took away that it's not so much about the lyrics as it is about the way the beats feel, so what drives this album is the production.

influences.name: J Dilla
influences.context: It's about me returning back to the original style of music that I once did, you know. Not saying that I have moved away from that style of music, which is sample-based, J Dilla-esque, psychedelic hip-hop, Wu-Tang influence.

influences.name: Wu-Tang Clan
influences.context: It's about me returning back to the original style of music that I once did, you know. Not saying that I have moved away from that style of music, which is sample-based, J Dilla-esque, psychedelic hip-hop, Wu-Tang influence.

influences.name: David Bowie
influences.context: Look at somebody like Bowie. Look how he went out. I look at it like that.

influences.name: unspecified greats
influences.context: There's albums from then that still inspire me.

influences.name: Larry David
influences.context: What I learned from Larry David is how to make improv seem like it was written. Like a lot of the songs on this album.

influences.name: Ian Curtis
influences.context: But that's just growing up and seeing different artists. Somebody like Joy Division. He (Ian Curtis) did that with Closer, that's what he was doing, and we still listen to that album to this day.

influences.name: Ali Shaheed Muhammad
influences.context: You seem full of patience, with a perpetual awareness of yourself in the game. Is this something you learned from hanging with Ali Shaheed Muhammad? "I haven't talked to him in a long time. He has real strong, Islamic beliefs and shit. I guess the biggest thing he was telling me at that time... his big deal was always like – 'you can say whatever you want, it's just about how you say it, learning ways to say it'."

influences.name: Nas
influences.context: If it wasn't for Nas, would I be doing this?

influences.name: LL Cool J
influences.context: After his cousin babysat him and introduced him to LL Cool J's Radio, the young boy born Daniel Sewell in West Detroit was hooked.

influences.name: MF Doom
influences.context: "That was the worst experience of my life," he tells me. "Not necessarily me being locked up or that my freedom was gone, but that I couldn't pick the music that I wanted to listen to. That hurt more than anything. I used to have my brother mail me MF Doom lyrics just so I could have something."

influences.name: Julia Cameron
influences.context: To do so, he turned to Julia Cameron's The Artist's Way – the famous guide on unlocking creativity and building artistic self-confidence. He liked it even more when he discovered the book was inspired by Cameron's journey with recovering from addiction: "I already resonated with that, because that's why I'm reading this fucking book!"

influences.name: Cynthoni
influences.context: That's all the more refined with the eight-minute epic 'The End', produced by Cynthoni (formerly Sewerslvt) – an elusive producer who ushered in a new wave of visceral, provocative breakcore in the early 2020s. "They capture an emotion without lyrics, it's amazing," Brown gushes.

influences.name: Marvin Gaye
influences.context: You look at albums that stand the test of time, like Marvin Gaye's What's Going On. That's like a time capsule for that period. We listen to that and could relate to that shit to this day. I don't know if I got What's Going On's in my discography yet, but that's what I'm striving for.

influences.name: The Streets
influences.context: Can you give me three non-negotiable albums you think everyone should listen to? The Streets, A Grand Don't Come for Free. That's audio cinema. If anybody likes deep dives of concept albums, that's the greatest to me.
